Case Vignette: James

James is a 68-year-old married man who has worked as a school counselor for over three decades. He presents as a thoughtful, measured individual, though his hands tremble slightly as he adjusts the collar of his polo shirt during our sessions. He describes himself as someone who has always been "the listener," the calm presence in a storm of adolescent crises.

The event that changed everything happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late October. James had stayed late at the middle school where he works, meeting with a student who was struggling with bullying. The sun was already low, casting long shadows across the empty parking lot. As he walked toward his car, a man emerged from between two vans. James remembers the smell of stale beer and the sound of gravel crunching under boots. The man demanded his wallet. James complied immediately, but the man struck him twice-once across the jaw, once in the ribs-before fleeing.

In the weeks that followed, James did not tell his wife the full story. He said he'd been mugged, but minimized the violence. He returned to work after three days, convinced that routine would restore him. But the school hallways no longer felt familiar. The laughter of students became jarring, unpredictable. He began arriving an hour early so he could park directly in front of the main entrance. He started scanning the faces of parents at pickup, cataloging them for threat.

The nightmares began in November. They are not replays of the assault, but variations-the man's face morphing into the faces of students he has counseled, the parking lot stretching into an endless corridor. He wakes at 3:17 AM most nights, his jaw clenched so tightly that his molars ache. His wife, a retired nurse, has learned not to touch him when he startles. "I feel like I'm living inside a bell jar," he told me once. "Everything is muffled, but also too loud."

At work, James has become hypervigilant in ways that concern his colleagues. He insisted on installing a panic button in his office, citing "safety protocols." He now conducts all meetings with his door slightly ajar, a behavior he justifies as "transparency." But he knows the truth: he needs an exit. He has stopped walking through the gymnasium during basketball games, avoiding the echo of sneakers on hardwood because it sounds too much like running footsteps.

His marriage has grown strained. He and his wife used to take evening walks along the river near their home. Now he refuses, citing back pain from the old injury. But the real reason is that he cannot tolerate the sensation of being watched. He has begun carrying a small pocketknife, something he never did before. He feels ashamed of this, but the shame does not override the compulsion.

The most painful change, James says, is the way he now sees the students he serves. For thirty-four years, he has believed in the fundamental goodness of children. Now, when a seventh-grader slams a locker in anger, James feels his chest tighten. When a boy with a hoodie walks too quickly down the hall, James's vision narrows. He has started documenting "concerning behaviors" in a notebook he keeps locked in his desk. He knows this is not who he was. He knows this is not who he wants to be.

He told me recently, "I used to think I understood pain. I spent my whole career helping kids through theirs. But I never knew what it meant to be afraid in your own skin. Now I do. And I don't know how to give that back."
